artboards.title: Homepage · paste a link + icon grid

annotations.text:
Homepage — top half pastes a link, bottom half is the icon grid.
The paste box is shaped like a youtube-to-mp4 site, with one change: it resolves the link against a CONNECTED channel and refuses anything that is not yours. That keeps the primary-source rule you set, and keeps you off the pattern that got the youtube-mp3 sites sued.
The 16 icon tiles are live — hover raises the play button, click fires it. Locked tiles refuse.

Consumer · Landing — the main entry point.
Hero, then Popular this week with image icons, then a quick-fire row. Every card and chip is live: hover raises the play button, click fires the sound.
The creator door is deliberately small — a 'For creators' button in the nav and one strip at the foot. Consumers never have to step over an upload flow to get to a sound.

Consumer · Soundboard — click the pads, they make noise.
15 pads, hover to raise the play button, click to fire. The four PRO pads refuse and show what they cost you instead. The bottom bar tracks what last played.
The sounds are synthesised blips standing in for real audio — the interaction is real, the audio is a placeholder.

Two doors, one product:
· Consumers land here, on the board.
· Creators enter through 'For creators' → the upload flow on the next page.
A creator is also a consumer, so the creator path is additive — it never replaces this nav.

1 · Source and trim
Creators upload footage they hold, and the card image is a FRAME OF THAT SAME FILE — which is where the streamer picture and the motion loop come from. No separate avatar upload, no third-party art.
The 30s cap and the trim range are the only things published; the source video is never shown in the library.

2 · Rights check
Three questions and a signature, filed with the sound. Two of the answers are dead ends by design — someone else's clip stops the upload, and declared music sends you back to trim — because both are cheaper to catch here than after publication.
The right-hand record is what the product can point to later; none of it appears on the public card.

Open questions on this flow, for you:
· Spot-check after publish (drawn here) or review before? Pre-review kills the upload-to-live loop but caps exposure.
· Do you want a written-permission upload field for the third option, or drop that option entirely and take own-footage only?
· Withdrawal is drawn as immediate and reason-free. Confirm that is the policy you want.

A · Studio Rack — the direction the consumer and creator screens are built in.
Dark, dense, tool-like. Filenames in mono are the primary text; PRO is a small outlined tag, never a paywall billboard.
Tradeoff: reads as pro software, which may undersell the fun of the content.

B · Paper Catalogue
Carries the palette and type from your market-overview doc (warm paper, signal orange, Archivo / Source Serif / JetBrains Mono). Rows, not tiles — the fastest way to scan filenames, and it puts the creator's name in the sentence.
Tradeoff: least visual; the streamer picture shrinks to a 52px thumb, so GIFs stop being the draw.

C · Cassette
Maximalist and physical — thick ink borders, hard offset shadows, sticker badges. Locked cards are hatched over rather than dimmed, so PAID reads as a texture across the grid.
Tradeoff: loudest to build and to live with; the style has to survive 248 items without becoming noise.

D · Poster Grid
Image-first: edge-to-edge tiles, one hairline between them, chrome reduced to text. The streamer's face is the interface; the filename sits on a scrim.
Tradeoff: metadata is cramped by design — long filenames truncate early, and free vs paid is a small dot vs a small lock.

Four directions for the sound library.
Same eight sounds and the same free/paid split in each, so only the design changes.
One card in every direction is shown mid-playback.
Still unpicked — A is leading, which is why the consumer and creator screens use it.
